label: position 2 (third original token)
explanation: Positional feature: fires on every sequence exactly at step t=2, the third original input token, regardless of token identity or sequence length (rate 1.000 at t=2; precision 1.0). Magnitude is nearly constant (median 0.355, max 0.427); the top activations come from particular prefixes (e.g. 3 w a). It does not fire at other original positions, at the delimiter, or during the copy phase. The only misses are weak activations (~0.25 of max): at t=1 when the first token is v, and occasionally at t=3. Together these hold 0.3% of the activation mass.

issues: The claims hold up. On the test split, 't == 2' scores precision 1.0, recall 0.990, F1 0.995 and mass recall 0.997, with no false positives. On the dev split, t=2 fires in 500000 of 500000 sequences (rate 1.000). The median activation is 0.355 and the max is 0.427, with the top examples all from the prefix '3 w a'.
'Does not fire at the delimiter or in the copy phase' is very nearly true. On dev it fires 8 times at the delimiter and once in the copy phase, out of about 3.2M steps. That is negligible.

Small imprecision: the explanation says the t=1 misses happen 'when the first token is v', but this needs the second token as well. The predicate (t==1)&(first_tok==tok('v')) has precision 0.26, so only about a quarter of v-first sequences fire at t=1, at about 0.25 of max. These misses hold 0.3% of the activation mass.

Adding that case gives (t==2)|((t==1)&(first_tok==tok('v'))). This raises mass recall to 0.9998 but lowers test F1 to 0.987, because of 12423 false positives. So the simple predicate t==2 is the better one.

The remaining misses are about 400 weak activations (about 0.26 of max) at t=3. They are scattered and hold about 0% of the mass. No systematic counterexample class by token, length or history remains.
